2  Dataset3 (breast 1.6M cells) tutorial (BPCells used)

library(BPCells)
library(SingleCellMQC)
Note on Disk Space Management (BPCells Mode)

When operating in BPCells mode, certain processing steps will generate a temp directory within your current working folder. These temporary files may not always be automatically deleted upon completion. To prevent excessive disk space consumption, we strongly recommend manually removing the temp directory once the Quality Control (QC) pipeline has finished. We are working on optimizing this workflow in the next release to handle temporary file cleanup automatically.

2.1 Data import

To optimize memory efficiency and handle large-scale datasets, we utilize the BPCells-based storage mode. This approach minimizes RAM usage by performing operations on-disk. You can define the storage path for the data using the dir_BPCells parameter.

dir_GEX <- paste0("/data/SingleCellMQC/GSE235326/", dir("/data/SingleCellMQC/GSE235326/"))
gsm_part <- gsub(".*/(GSM\\d+)_(hbca_c\\d+).*", "\\1", dir_GEX)
hbca_part <- gsub(".*/(GSM\\d+)_(hbca_c\\d+).*", "\\2", dir_GEX)
breast <- Read10XH5Data(dir_GEX = dir_GEX, sample = hbca_part, dir_BPCells = "/project/largedata/GSE235326_BP/", min.cells=1)

The metadata for this dataset is sourced from the CellxGene Census. We have previously downloaded this metadata, filtered for relevant columns, and merged it into the breast object. For brevity, the filtering logic is omitted here, and we proceed by loading the consolidated RDS object.

# load add metadata object
breast_process <- readRDS("./breast.rds")

2.2 Preprocessing before QC

2.2.1 QC Metrics calculation

# Calculate the information of QC metrics. 
breast_process <- CalculateMetrics(breast_process)

2.2.2 Sctype main clusters annotation (only for qc)

It contains T cells, B cells, NK cells, DC cells, Mon / Mac cells, endothelial cells, fibroblasts, granulocytes and other cells (erythrocytes, epithelial cells, etc.).

Important

This automated annotation provides a sufficient general overview for an initial quality control assessment of your samples. However, for in-depth biological analysis requiring high precision, it is strongly recommended to perform detailed manual cell type annotation, as the accuracy of automated methods can be limited.

# For each sample, the cells were annotated separately.
breast_process <- RunScType(breast_process, split.by="orig.ident")
# interactive table
PlotSampleCellTypePCT(breast_process, sample.by = "orig.ident", celltype.by = "ScType", return.type="interactive_table")
## Loading required namespace: SeuratObject

CellType% per Sample

2.3 Sex verification

To avoid potential recording mistakes and data transmission errors, checking whether the file labeling is consistent with analyzed data features is necessary at the beginning of sample QC. By default, you can check if your sample gender information is incorrectly labeled. In addition, if your sample does not have gender information, you can get it according to the table below. Use PlotSampleLabel() to visualise the percentage of gene expression, with gender-related genes set as the default.

# interactive table
out<-PlotSampleLabel(breast_process, return.type = "interactive_table" )
out

The pct of features

Note

The analyzed sex results: Female: 167 ; Male: 0 ;

2.4 Low quality cells detection

## `split.by` can be set to sample or batch information, etc., to explore the number of low-quality cells detected in different groups.
breast_process <- RunLQ_MAD(breast_process, split.by = "orig.ident", nmads = 3)
breast_process <- RunLQ_ddqc(breast_process, split.by = "orig.ident")
# fixed coutoff get from paper
breast_process <- RunLQ_fixed(breast_process, min.nCount_RNA = 500, min.nFeature_RNA = 200, percent.mt = 10, percent.rb = 50)

2.5 Doublets Detection

Time and Memory

The following metrics were recorded during the processing of this dataset to provide a reference for performance (167 breast tissue samples, 1.6M cells):

Method Execution Time Peak Memory (RAM)
cxds 25.11 min 1.57 GB
hybrid 69.66 min 10.72 GB
bcds 121.87 min 7.81 GB
scDblFinder 181.10 min 3.30 GB
DoubletFinder 997.17 min 10.05 GB 
breast_process <- RunDbt_scDblFinder(breast_process, split.by = "orig.ident", do.topscore = T)
breast_process <- RunDbt_cxds(breast_process, split.by = "orig.ident")
breast_process <- RunDbt_bcds(breast_process, split.by = "orig.ident")
breast_process <- RunDbt_hybrid(breast_process, split.by = "orig.ident")
breast_process <- RunDbt_DoubletFinder(breast_process, split.by = "orig.ident")

To aid in method selection, SingleCellMQC evaluates the influence of doublet removal on clustering performance using five metrics: Average Silhouette Width (ASW), Calinski-Harabasz index (CH), Davies-Bouldin Index (DBI), Adjusted Rand Index (ARI), and Normalized Mutual Information (NMI).

Important

It is crucial to note that this step is very time-consuming and should be considered an auxiliary strategy rather than a mandatory one. Users who do not require this evaluation can opt to skip this step.

breast_process_bench_out <- RunBenchmarkDoublet(breast_process, split.by = "orig.ident",
                                      method_columns =c("db_scDblFinder", "db_cxds", "db_bcds","db_hybrid", "db_DoubletFinder") )
PlotBenchmarkDoublet(breast_process_bench_out)$plot
Note

The scDbFinder method achieved the highest overall ranking, outperforming other methods in Dataset 3.

2.6 Summary Sample QC Information

This section provides a concise summary of the key quality control (QC) metrics, generated via the SummarySample function, derived from initial basic processing steps. It allows for a rapid overview of critical sample quality indicators. For a more detailed breakdown of individual QC analyses, please refer to the another chapter. Below is a description of the columns presented in the summary table:

# interactive table
# summary sample qc results
summaryinteractive <- SummarySample(breast_process, sample.by ="orig.ident", tissue = "breast", celltype.by = "ScType",
                              db_filter_columns = "db_scDblFinder",
                              lq_filter_columns = c("lq_fixed", "lq_RNA_gene_3mad", "lq_RNA_mt_3mad", "lq_RNA_umi_3mad"),
                              return.type ="interactive_table")
## 2026-03-13 11:18:41 ------CalculateMetricsPerSample.count
## 2026-03-13 11:18:52 ------CalculateMetricsPerSample.summary
summaryinteractive

2.7 Batch effect

2.7.1 Pseudobulk

Note

In this workflow, we analyze the impact of four specific covariates: sample_source, sequencing_platform, procedure_group, and age_group. This helps us determine whether these factors introduce significant batch effects.

Pseudobulk <- RunPseudobulkData(breast_process, assay = "RNA", slot = "counts", sample.by = "orig.ident",
                                other_cols_contain = c("sample_source", "sequencing_platform",  "procedure_group", "age_group"))

2.7.1.1 PCA

At the pseudobulk sample level, SingleCellMQC aggregates single-cell counts to generate pseudobulk profiles and performs PCA to evaluate the batch effects across samples. Variance decomposition of principal component scores further quantifies the contribution of each covariate (e.g., platform, donor, library batch) to sample-level variation.

PlotReducedDim(Pseudobulk, group.by = "sample_source", size = 1)
PlotReducedDim(Pseudobulk, group.by = "sequencing_platform", size = 1)
PlotReducedDim(Pseudobulk, group.by = "procedure_group", size = 1)

PCs variance decomposition analysis

varpart_pca <- RunVarPartPseudobulkPCA(Pseudobulk, variables = c("sample_source", "sequencing_platform", "procedure_group",  "age_group") )
## 11:19:42-------- runPseudobulkPCA
PlotVarPartStackBar(varpart_pca)
Note

In the Dataset 3, the pseudobulk sample PCA plot and variance decomposition analysis revealed that sequencing platform and sample source were the major contributors to sample-level variation.

2.7.1.2 Per-feature Variance Partition (all cells)

In addition, SingleCellMQC applies a linear mixed model to each feature in the pseudobulk data to estimate per-feature variance attributable to each covariate, enabling insights into the main drivers of batch effects.

VarPart <- RunVarPartPseudobulk(Pseudobulk, variables = c("sample_source", "sequencing_platform", "procedure_group", "age_group")  )
median(VarPart$procedure_group)
## [1] 9.487758e-13
median(VarPart$sequencing_platform)
## [1] 0.3401251
median(VarPart$age_group)
## [1] 0.001121889
PlotVarPartVln(VarPart)
Note

Per-feature variance decomposition analysis further confirmed that sequencing platform was the strongest driver of expression variability, accounting for a median of 34.0% of variance, which was substantially greater than biologically relevant variables such as age (median 0.1%) or procedure group (median ~0%).

2.7.1.3 Per-feature Variance Partition (each celltype)

## Pseudobulk by celltype
PseudobulkCellType <- RunPseudobulkData(breast_process, assay = "RNA", slot = "counts", sample.by = "orig.ident", cluster.by = "ScType",
                                        other_cols_contain = c("sample_source", "sequencing_platform", "procedure_group",  "age_group"))
VarPartCellType <- RunVarPartPseudobulk(PseudobulkCellType, variables = c("sample_source", "sequencing_platform", "procedure_group",  "age_group")  )
PlotVarPartVln(VarPartCellType, do.split = T)
Note

We also performed variance decomposition within individual cell types and find that, in most cases, sequencing platform and sample source remained the dominant batch-associated covariates.

2.7.2 Single-cell UMAP

## preprocess
breast_process <- RunPipeline(breast_process, preprocess = "rna.umap")
PlotReducedDim(breast_process, split.by = "sequencing_platform", ncol = 3)+
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "none")
Note

Further analysis at the cellular level revealed significant heterogeneity between different sequencing platforms, suggesting that sequencing platform may be the primary source of batch effects

2.7.3 Feature-level (GTE scores)

At the feature level, SingleCellMQC integrates the group technical effects (GTE ) scores to assess the influence of batch covariates on individual features, enabling the identification of features that are influenced by technical variations.

breast_process = RunBatchGTE(breast_process, assay = "RNA", group.by = "ScType", batch.by = "sequencing_platform")
PlotGTEBar(breast_process, ntop = 10)
Note

The top 10 genes are predominantly mitochondrial (MTRNR2L12, MT-ND3, MT-ATP6), ribosomal (RPS17, RPL31, RPL36A), and dissociation/stress-related (JUND) genes

2.8 Generate QC HTML report

The RunReport function compiles all QC results into a HTML document containing interactable plots, tables, and QC warnings across sample-, cell-, feature-, and batch-levels.

RunReport(breast_process,
          tissue = "breast",
          sample.by = "orig.ident",
          RNA.batch.by = c("sequencing_platform","procedure_group", "sample_source"),
          RNA_cluster_name = "rna_cluster",
          RNA.covariate.formula = ~ (1|sequencing_platform) + (1|procedure_group) + (1|sample_source),
          outputFile = "../Dataset3_html/SingleCellMQC.html"
)
